About

A practitioner-informed approach: the dancer’s body as an archive the written record leaves out.

Anisha Ahuja is a cultural studies scholar whose work historicizes Indian “modern classical” dance, with a focus on Kathak and the Lucknow gharana. Her research asks how the hereditary performers and Mughal courtesans (tawa’if) who shaped these forms were classified, marginalized and finally absented, and how that absence still structures dance education, gesture and national identity today.

She works between Cultural Studies and Gender Studies, drawing on feminist and postcolonial theory, archival research in the British Library’s India Office Records, and her own embodied training as a Kathak dancer and teacher. The result is a method she calls spectral gesture analysis: following the courtesan’s traces across centuries of sources through the gestures that outlived her.

She holds a B.A. in Political Science and Feminist Studies from the University of California, Santa Barbara (2015) and an M.A. in Cultural Studies from CGU (2020). She has spent over a decade in political scholarship and education, teaching thesis and dissertation writing at CGU, as an adjunct at the University of La Verne, and as Senior Writing Consultant at CGU’s Center for Writing and Rhetoric, where she also chairs the Anti-Discrimination Committee across the seven Claremont Colleges. Before her doctoral work she was editorial assistant to the Keywords Feminist Editorial Collective at NYU Press. Alongside her academic work she trains and teaches Kathak at Nrityanvita Kathak Academy.

Research threads

01

Gesture as archive

Hand, eye and foot movements carry history. Reading mudras, gats and footwork as genealogies that record who was erased from the form.

02

Empire & the “nautch girl”

How European travel writing and colonial sanitation policy turned the courtesan into a category of deviance and disease.

03

Nationalism & revival

How the anti-nautch movement and post-independence Akademies rebuilt Kathak as a Sanskritized, respectable, “classical” institution.

04

Diaspora & pedagogy

Examination syllabi and riyaz as the channels through which national narratives reach dancers in the US and UK.

05

Disembodiment

A counter-concept to embodiment: what the classical dancer’s body materially removes in order to perform.

06

Popular culture

From Air India’s “Safety Mudras” to Heeramandi, the courtesan returns in media exactly when the nation needs her.

Doctoral dissertation · Claremont Graduate University · 2026 · 254 pages · CGU Dissertation Fellowship Award 2024–25

Haunted Movements

Indian “Modern Classical” Dance, Disembodiment and the Spectral Courtesan

A practitioner-informed history of how the courtesan was spectralized across the British Raj, Indian nationalism and the postcolonial cultural institution, and how her ghost is still invoked every time a dancer ties on her bells.

From the archive

Figures from the dissertation: eighteenth- and nineteenth-century paintings and documents in which the courtesan survives as trace. Photographs of British Library material by the author. Full image credits →

A long spectralization

The arc the dissertation follows, from early European encounters to the present.

1770s – 1850s
European travel writings describe “nautch parties,” recasting courtesan performance as spectacle and sexual curiosity.
1860s – 1880s
Contagious Diseases Acts and lock hospitals. Sanitary and military proceedings in the North-Western Provinces and Oudh classify “dancing girls” through venereal disease policy.
1890s – 1930s
The anti-nautch movement. Christian Literature Society tracts and early Hindu reformers (Brahmo Samaj, Arya Samaj) define a sexual Other through the courtesan’s ankle bells, painted hands and jewelry.
1925
Fourth All-India Music Conference, Lucknow. Revival discourse frames Lucknow’s performance culture as lewd and in need of reform.
Post-1947
Akademies and examination syllabi. Kathak is standardized as “classical,” its Mughal and courtesan histories abstracted and Sanskritized.
2024
Air India’s “Safety Mudras” and Netflix’s Heeramandi. The courtesan returns as brand, feminist icon and caricature at once.
Haunted Movements: Indian “Modern Classical” Dance, Disembodiment and the Spectral Courtesan
    Overview

    What this dissertation argues

    The absence of the courtesan is not an accident of history. It is the ground on which Indian “modern classical” dance was built, and it still does ideological work.

    The dissertation historicizes Kathak and the other Indian “modern classical” dances against the Mughal courtesans (tawa’if) and hereditary performers whose absence they are built on. Removing and re-packaging the courtesan, it argues, is one of the ways Indian dance mobilizes Hindu nationalist sentiment inside the “classical” dancer herself. Rather than a lost origin, the courtesan is followed as a spectral figure, traceable through colonial archives, reform tracts, revival conferences, exam syllabi and the gestures a diasporic dancer still performs every week.

    Key concepts

    Spectral gesture analysis

    The project’s method: following the courtesan’s traces, mentions and hauntings across non-periodized sources through gesture.

    Archaic modernity

    Banu Subramaniam’s term for the paradox at the heart of Hindu nationalism: the ancient and the modern claimed at once.

    Gestural genealogy

    Usha Iyer’s concept, used to recover the corporeal histories carried by movement vocabularies.

    Disembodiment

    A proposed alternative to “embodiment”: what the classical dancer’s body materially erases to reproduce the institution.

    Sanskritization

    The re-attachment of syncretic, erotic courtesan practice to Vedic texts like the Natyasastra.

    Haunting

    After Avery Gordon: an affective, “transformative recognition” rather than cold knowledge.

    Introduction

    Haunted Movements & the Spectral Courtesan

    …every time one ‘dresses up’, wears the dance costume, jewelry and ties the bells around one’s feet, the figure of the historical hereditary dancing woman of the past is being invoked, consciously or unconsciously.Nrithya Pillai, quoted as epigraph

    The introduction opens with Air India’s 2024 “Safety Mudras” film, in which classical dancers mime seatbelt and oxygen-mask instructions as if they were new mudras. It is read as the whole project in miniature: a nation presenting itself through gendered “classical” dance, and claiming Vedic authenticity and global modernity in the same gesture, the paradox Banu Subramaniam calls archaic modernity.

    The project bridges Cultural Studies and Gender Studies with a method that pairs postcolonial archival reading with the author’s own embodied training. Following Veena Oldenburg, the tawa’if are treated as resistant, non-heteronormative communities, not only victims. Because the courtesan survives mainly as trace, archival sources and dance practice are read together to locate her.

    Sources surveyedEuropean travel writings (1777–1855); India Office Records proceedings on venereal disease policy; Christian Literature Society anti-nautch tracts; the 1925 Fourth All-India Music Conference report; contemporary Akademi syllabi; archival paintings; film and streaming media.
    Methodology

    Spectral gesture analysis

    A way of reading that is attuned to the figure the archive exiles, using the gestures she left behind to connect sources that chronology keeps apart.

    Spectral gesture analysis centers the demonized historical dancer and uses her gestures as bridges between sources that chronology keeps apart: travel journals, sanitary proceedings, tracts, syllabi, film. It assumes the courtesan was disfigured into a ghost by signification and synecdoche, and reads for the trace.

    Theoretical lineage

    • Deconstructive historiography (Gayatri Spivak): attending to what material interests, ideologies and methods are at stake in historical writing, and allowing oneself to be haunted by discontinuity and messy chronology.
    • Haunting (Avery Gordon): a sensuous, affective knowledge; being haunted is a “transformative recognition,” not cold knowledge.
    • The archive as absence (Gyanendra Pandey, Durba Mitra, Anjali Arondekar): figures not silenced but exiled within the archive, produced as trifling so that the archive can stand as Reason and State.
    • Gestural genealogy (Usha Iyer): corporeal histories recovered through movement vocabularies.
    • Stickiness (Sara Ahmed): how particular gestures accumulate national and colonial affect.

    Practitioner position

    The author writes as a Lucknow-gharana Kathak dancer and instructor certified through Akademi examinations. That position is the entry point: the spectralization of the courtesan becomes perceptible in salamis, amads, costume, and the “Mughal influences” named in class but rarely explained.

    Chapter 1

    Dancing in the Diaspora and the Gestural Abstraction of Tawa’if in Nationalized Pedagogy

    Time-folding warps are one of the critical ingredients of Hindu nationalism.Banu Subramaniam, Holy Science, as chapter epigraph

    The chapter starts from the diasporic Kathak student, whose knowledge is certified by exams written by post-independence Akademies and sent abroad as the “homeland’s” version of the form, folding religious and historical narrative into daily riyaz.

    Sources

    • The report of the Fourth All-India Music Conference, Lucknow, 1925.
    • The curriculum of contemporary state-sponsored Kathak institutions and Akademi examination syllabi.

    Argument

    Kathak is fundamentally pedagogical: pedagogy links the national, the transnational and the historical, and licenses the label “modern classical.” Its formation is an apparatus that (1) produces modernity through performance education, (2) re-wires gender by removing courtesans from local practice, and (3) writes a dominant history that erases Muslim culture from Kathak’s past.

    Revival is thus structured by archaic modernity and keeps marginalizing the subaltern. Yet the tawa’if persists in gesture and space: face and eye movement, the circular travel and handling of dress shaped by intimate rooms, and her place in the economy of Nawabi Awadh.

    Chapter 2

    The “Dancing Girl” and Subjectivation at the Site of Performance and Empire

    Two bodies of material are read together: European travel writing about “nautch girls,” and India Office Records proceedings on venereal-disease policy applied to “dancing girls.”

    Sources

    • Journals and memoirs by Jemima Kindersley (1777), James Forbes, Maria Callcott, Reginald Heber, Anne Elwood, Thomas Skinner, Emma Roberts and William Knighton, among others.
    • The “Proceedings and Consultations of the Government of India and of its Presidencies and Provinces, 1702–1945,” narrowed to Home Proceedings and the North-Western Provinces, Agra and Oudh, across the Departments of Sanitation, Military, and Agriculture, Revenue and Commerce.
    • The Contagious Diseases Act of 1868 and annual reports of lock hospitals at Lucknow and Sitapur.

    Argument

    Colonial governance turned courtesans into “prostitute classes,” tying their cultural role to deviant sexuality through hygiene and high-caste respectability. Encountered as a representative of India, the courtesan was emptied into the categories “nautch girl” and “dancing girl,” which captured anxieties about sexuality and culture and licensed disciplinary policy. Her signifiers hardened into a sign for deviance and national threat.

    Chapter 3

    The “Nautch Girl” and the Shaping of Gendered Ideology in India

    The anti-nautch movement, a reform campaign running from the late nineteenth century into the 1930s, enforced the cultural and financial marginalization of courtesans.

    Sources

    • The India Office Records’ subcollection of Christian Literature Society tracts.
    • Related social reform materials from the Brahmo Samaj and Arya Samaj.

    Argument

    In the tracts the courtesan appears by metonymy: ankle bells, red-painted hands and feet, jewelry, music. Through those parts, vice and temptation were attached to “nautch girls,” and early Hindu nationalists used the result to define the nation’s sexual Other just as respectable performance forms were emerging.

    Why metonymy mattersThe same bells, hands and jewelry that the tracts condemned are the ones a classical dancer now ties on and paints before performing. The chapter sets up the gestural analysis of Chapter 4 by showing how these signs were first charged with moral meaning.
    Chapter 4

    Gestures That Disembody and the Sanskritization of Tawa’if Culture

    Written from a practitioner’s perspective and using Usha Iyer’s gestural genealogy, the chapter examines Kathak elements tied to a distorted use of the Natyasastra alongside the mujra as the archive depicts it.

    Argument

    The contemporary classical dancer takes part in the material Sanskritization of courtesan culture at the level of gesture. Against “embodiment,” the chapter proposes disembodiment: through the form itself, dancers erase courtesan histories of syncretism and eroticism, reproducing Kathak as an institution for a global market.

    A written choreography

    The chapter closes with a written choreography that sets Natyasastra concepts such as srngara (the erotic sentiment) against colonial descriptions and contemporary pedagogy, using specific gestures to unveil what text and image leave out, and offering gesture itself as a method.

    Conclusion

    Gajagamini Gat (Elephant Walk) & the Neoliberal Courtesan

    The method is tested on one gesture: the gajagamini gat, the elephant walk, performed by Bibbojaan in Bhansali’s Heeramandi (2024).

    A gesture with a lineage

    A gat is a stylized walk from the Mughal era, much practiced in Awadh; the elephant walk recurs from Mughal-e-Azam (1960) to Gaja Gamini (2000) and invokes the Kama Sutra’s Hastini.

    What the walk reveals

    Audiences read it as feminist and body-positive, and dancers copied it online. But the Vedic reference is invoked only selectively, stripped of the sex that defines the elephant woman, so as to serve archaic modernity, while the courtesan who performs it stays marginal and is cast out. The gat marks the courtesan’s latest transformation, now under neoliberalism; gesture remains a tool for thinking about India’s modernity, its fundamentalism, and its obsession with the courtesan.

    Sources

    Primary source overview

    Appendix A groups the dissertation’s primary materials by type. The sources span three centuries and are deliberately read against chronology.

    Written observations from Europeans in India
    Travel journals, memoirs and letters, 1777–1855. Kindersley, Forbes, Callcott, Heber, Elwood, Skinner, Roberts, Knighton; Solvyns’ Les Hindous plate “Nautch. A Hindoo Dance” (1808); Dyson’s compiled “Impressions of Indian Dancing and Music.”
    Archival government or policy texts
    India Office Records and Private Papers, British Library. The 1868 Contagious Diseases Act; annual lock-hospital reports for Lucknow Cantonments and Sitapur; Sanitary Commissioner reviews on venereal disease among British soldiers; Home, North-Western Provinces, Agra and Oudh proceedings; Elizabeth Garrett Anderson’s 1870 enquiry.
    Archival social reform materials
    Christian Literature Society tracts and anti-nautch movement publications, late nineteenth to early twentieth century, alongside the 1925 Fourth All-India Music Conference report.
    Archival paintings
    Lucknow and Mughal miniatures from the British Library (Add Or 2659, 3261, 1520) and the Cleveland Museum of Art, and Solvyns’ 1808 etchings. Visual depictions of nautch and courtesan performance used to trace metonymic markers: bells, painted hands, jewelry, dress and spatial arrangement.
    Media sources
    Air India’s “Safety Mudras” (2024); Heeramandi: The Diamond Bazaar (2024); Mughal-e-Azam (1960); Gaja Gamini (2000); Devdas; Wajid Ali Shah’s Bani; contemporary Akademi syllabi.

      Book review · Women’s Studies, 2020

      The Diagnosis of a Regime

      A review of Banu Subramaniam, Holy Science: The Biopolitics of Hindu Nationalism (University of Washington Press, 2019), published in Women’s Studies: An inter-disciplinary journal.

      CitationAhuja, Anisha. “The Diagnosis of a Regime.” Review of Holy Science: The Biopolitics of Hindu Nationalism, by Banu Subramaniam. Women’s Studies 49, no. 5 (2020): 553–555. Published online 22 July 2020. doi:10.1080/00497878.2020.1785220

      The review appeared in the same year the author completed her M.A. in Cultural Studies and began doctoral work. Its title frames Subramaniam’s book as a diagnosis: an account of how a political regime makes religion and science speak for each other. The three pages that follow set out what the book argues, how its central concept was carried into the author’s later work, and where to find the review.

      Where to read it.
      Book review · The Diagnosis of a Regime

      The book under review

      Holy Science is a study of how Hindu nationalism in contemporary India fuses religious orthodoxy with the authority and vocabulary of modern science. Published in the University of Washington Press series Feminist Technosciences, it reads Hindutva as a biopolitical project: a politics that governs bodies, reproduction, gender and the environment by presenting Vedic tradition as already scientific and science as already Vedic.

      Subramaniam names the paradox at the centre of this project archaic modernity: an ancient, timeless civilisation and a technologically ascendant nation-state are claimed in the same breath, and each is used to legitimate the other. She describes the “time-folding warps” through which the past is collapsed into the present as one of the critical ingredients of Hindu nationalism.

      The book is written from a feminist science-studies position and insists that the biological, the religious and the political cannot be separated into tidy domains. It is this refusal of separation, and the concept of archaic modernity in particular, that the dissertation takes up.

      NoteThis page summarises the book, not the review. The review’s own text is available through the journal; see Access & citation.
      Book review · The Diagnosis of a Regime

      From a review to a method

      The concept the review engaged in 2020 became the organizing paradox of Haunted Movements in 2026.

      Across the dissertation, archaic modernity is the lens through which each new source is read:

      • Introduction. Air India’s 2024 “Safety Mudras” film is read as a visual representation of the paradox between the ancient and the modern that is central to India’s brand of nationalism, with Subramaniam cited directly. Read →
      • Chapter 1. Opens with the “time-folding warps” epigraph and argues that twentieth-century revival of Kathak was structured through a framework of archaic modernity that continued the marginalization of subaltern figures. Read →
      • Chapter 4. The Sanskritization of courtesan gesture is treated as archaic modernity enacted in the dancer’s own body. Read →
      • Conclusion. The gajagamini gat in Heeramandi recalls the Kama Sutra selectively, only insofar as the reference serves archaic modernity and not the sex and pleasure the text actually describes. Read →

      Subramaniam also appears in the dissertation’s wider conversation: her essay on “Biology” (with Angie Willey) sits in the same Keywords volume to which the author contributed a year after the review.

      From September 2019 to December 2020, working from Pomona College, she was editorial assistant to the collective that produced the book: providing administrative support, managing contracts for its seventy contributors, tracking the development of each chapter, organizing a focus group at the National Women’s Studies Association, and helping compile the final manuscript. The volume’s contributors page lists her as a PhD student in Cultural Studies and Women’s and Gender Studies at Claremont Graduate University. The two pages that follow describe the volume and map the entries that sit closest to her research.

      Edited volume · Keywords for Gender and Sexuality Studies

      The volume

      Following the model of Raymond Williams’s Keywords, each NYU Press volume gathers short essays on the vocabulary that organizes a field. Keywords for Gender and Sexuality Studies collects roughly seventy essays by scholars across the humanities and social sciences, from “#” and “Abjection” through “Woman,” and is accompanied by an open-access companion site hosting several web-only essays.

      The collection deliberately foregrounds Black, Indigenous and women of color feminisms; transnational feminisms; queer of color critique; trans, disability and fat studies; feminist science studies; and critiques of the state, law and prisons that emerge from queer and women of color justice movements. Many entries question the assumptions of humanism, from the racialized contours of property to eugenicist discourses of development, and reach for forms of relationality beyond settler-colonial and imperialist epistemologies.

      The collective’s own entry, “Race,” is credited to the Keywords Feminist Editorial Collective as a whole rather than to an individual, and the book’s production, coordinated across seventy contributors and a national focus group, reflects a collaborative mode of editing rather than single-author authority. Anisha Ahuja’s role sat at the centre of that coordination.

      Presentation · March 6, 2020 · Los Angeles

      19th Century Courtesans and Empire: Disciplinarity and Cultural Transformation as Sexual Violence

      Full-length paper at the UCLA Center for the Study of Women’s “Thinking Gender” graduate conference.

      Panel
      “Legacies of Empire and Settler Colonialism,” Session II
      Moderator
      Yogita Goyal, African American Studies and English, UCLA
      Programme title
      Listed as “Governmentality and Cultural Transformation as Sexual Violence”

      Where it leads

      This is the earliest public statement of the argument that became Chapter 2: that nineteenth-century colonial governance, through sanitation and military proceedings, reclassified courtesans as disciplined “dancing girls” and “prostitute classes,” and that this cultural transformation should be understood as a form of sexual violence rather than mere regulation. The archival base, the India Office Records’ proceedings on venereal disease policy in the North-Western Provinces and Oudh, is the same.

      Presentation · March 2020 · Claremont (cancelled)

      Rituals and Anti-Rites: Rituals of Nationalism and Heterotopic Spaces

      Paper accepted to the American Academy of Religion, Western Region; the conference was cancelled at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.

      Where it leads

      The pairing of ritual and nationalism anticipates the dissertation’s reading of Kathak training as ritualized practice through which Hindu nationalist narratives are embodied by diasporic dancers (Introduction, Chapter 1). “Heterotopic spaces,” Foucault’s term for real places that mirror and invert the surrounding order, points toward the dissertation’s attention to the courtesan’s own spaces: the kotha, the mujra, and the intimate room that shaped her circular movement.

      Presentation · April 28, 2021 · Claremont

      Performers and Performers-in-Space: Mughal-era Courtesans, Empire, and Counter-Coloniality

      CGU School of Arts and Humanities Forum.

      Where it leads

      The phrase “performers-in-space” names a concern that runs through the finished dissertation: the courtesan is not only a figure in texts but a body in a particular room, city and economy. Chapter 1 describes her gestural endurance and spatiality, her presence in the regional economy of the Nawabi city of Awadh, and the way her artistry shaped the environments she came into contact with. “Counter-coloniality” signals the reading, drawn from Veena Oldenburg, of tawa’if as non-heteronormative and resistant communities rather than victims only (Methodology).

      Keynote panel · November 12, 2021 · Online

      Subversion & Subterfuge in the Writing Center

      Keynote panelist, National Conference on Peer Tutoring in Writing.

      Context

      Drawn from the author’s work as Senior Consultant at CGU’s Center for Writing and Rhetoric, where she mentored writers across the Claremont Colleges and supported other graduate tutors. The title suggests the writing center as a site where institutional expectations can be quietly redirected, a theme consistent with her later NWSA panel on citational politics and feminist pedagogy, which critiqued the corporatization of university spaces and the appropriation of feminist knowledge.

      Presentation · February 17, 2022 · Santa Barbara

      The Shramik Special: COVID-19 Migrant Relief Trains in Lockdown India and Geographies of Domination

      American Literary and Urban Studies Conference.

      Context

      The Shramik Special trains were run by Indian Railways from May 2020 to move migrant workers stranded in cities by the national lockdown back to their home states. The paper’s subtitle, “geographies of domination,” reads this relief infrastructure as a spatial exercise of state power over labouring bodies. Though outside the dissertation’s period, it shares its concern with how the Indian state governs mobile, marginalized bodies through administrative systems, the same lens applied to colonial sanitary proceedings in Chapter 2.

      iPoster · August 31, 2017 · San Francisco

      Exploring Political Sustainability of Asian American Women in Elective Office

      With Pei-te Lien (first author). Annual Meeting of the American Political Science Association.

      Context

      The earliest item in the record, from the year after the author completed her B.A. in Political Science and Feminist Studies at UC Santa Barbara, where Pei-te Lien is Professor of Political Science. The project examined what sustains Asian American women’s careers in elected office. As a student researcher with Lien from 2016 to 2018 she interviewed elected officials, professors and activists in Southern California and Honolulu for a database of Asian Pacific American representation, work later featured in Lien and Nicole Filler’s Contesting the Last Frontier (Oxford University Press, 2022). It marks the political-science starting point from which her work moved toward cultural studies, gender studies and performance.

      Editing & writing consultation

      Finish the dissertation. Ship the manuscript.

      One-on-one consultation, developmental editing and copyediting for graduate students and academics, from someone who has spent six years at the Claremont Colleges doing exactly this.

      Enquire by email How it works
      Photo by Aaron Burden on Unsplash

      Services

      Three kinds of help, scoped to where the writing actually is.

      01

      Dissertation & thesis coaching

      Structure, argument and momentum: chapter plans, prospectus and proposal drafts, making sense of committee feedback, and the unstuck session when a chapter stalls. Weekly or fortnightly sessions with written notes after each.

      02

      Developmental editing

      Full-manuscript reads for articles and books: what the argument is, where it lands, what a reviewer will ask, and a revision plan. Includes a review of the revised draft.

      03

      Copyediting & professional documents

      Line-level editing to a style guide, citation cleanup, and the documents around the research: job letters, fellowship and grant applications, teaching and research statements, abstracts, conference proposals.

      Photos by Unseen Studio on Unsplash, lilartsy on Unsplash and Yannick Pulver on Unsplash

      Who this is for

      • Doctoral candidates in the humanities and social sciences, from prospectus to defense.
      • Master’s students finishing a thesis on a deadline.
      • Early-career academics turning a chapter into an article or a dissertation into a book.
      • Writers working in English as an additional language who want their argument to land as written.
      • Anyone applying for fellowships, grants or academic jobs who needs the documents to be as strong as the research.
      Why her
      • Senior Writing Consultant at CGU’s Center for Writing and Rhetoric since 2020; teaches Thesis and Dissertation Writing as adjunct faculty at CGU and the University of La Verne.
      • Trains and mentors new writing consultants; co-designed the center’s hiring and onboarding.
      • Editorial assistant to the NYU Press Keywords collective: seventy contributors, one manuscript, delivered.
      • Interdisciplinary by training (political science, feminist studies, cultural studies), so humanities and social-science writing both read as native.
      • Recently finished a 254-page dissertation herself. She knows what the last six months feel like.

      How it works

      Step 1

      Send a note

      What you’re writing, where it is, and your deadline. A paragraph is enough; attach a sample if you have one.

      Step 2

      A free 20-minute call

      To scope the work, agree a plan and a timeline, and make sure the fit is right in both directions.

      Step 3

      Editing or sessions on a schedule

      Fixed turnaround for edits; fixed session times for coaching. Written notes after every round so nothing lives only in conversation.

      Photo by Nick Morrison on Unsplash

      Questions people ask

      Will you write it for me?
      No. Coaching and editing make your writing clearer and your argument stronger; the ideas and the words stay yours, which is also what your university’s academic integrity policy requires.
      What about my field?
      Strongest in the humanities and interpretive social sciences: cultural studies, gender studies, history, performance, literature, politics, education. For quantitative or lab-science writing, the help is structural and stylistic rather than disciplinary.
      Style guides?
      Chicago, MLA and APA as standard; others by arrangement.
      Rates?
      Quoted after the scoping call, by the hour for coaching and by the manuscript for editing. Students are not charged the same as funded faculty.
      Confidentiality?
      Your work is never shared, quoted or used as an example without written permission.
